title: The human in the loop
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou and Wheadon recount two years of trying to use large language models for assessment, from the early prediction that teachers would soon get instant, accurate grades and feedback to the realisation that hallucinations made that impossible. Their argument is that LLM errors differ in kind from human errors, so the checks that catch human mistakes do not catch them, and a naive human reviewer of AI output is not enough. Editing AI feedback took teachers longer than writing it, and the self-driving-car analogy shows why human attention fails when errors are rare. Their answer is to redesign the process: teachers judge and record audio comments, AI transcribes and combines them, and comparative judgement handles grading. The piece ends with a free trial for English secondary schools, but the bulk is an argument about how to place humans in an AI workflow.
points: LLM hallucination is persistent and may be a feature rather than a bug, so decisions should not depend on it being fixed soon.
What matters is the type of error, not just the rate, because LLM mistakes are unlike human ones and escape systems built to catch human error.
A simple human-in-the-loop review fails: editing AI feedback took longer than writing it and rare errors lull reviewers into switching off.
Reworking the process, with teacher audio comments that AI transcribes and merges, mitigates hallucination while saving time.
Asking LLMs to compare essays rather than score them suits comparative judgement, which also standardises results across schools.
quotes: What matters is not just how many errors you make, but the type of error, and LLMs often make errors that humans would not make. This matters because many of the systems we use every day have tried and tested methods that catch and reduce human error, meaning that the overall system error can be much lower than the errors of the individual humans within it.

We don’t know how long it will take to completely solve hallucinations. We often hear that they will be fixed “soon”. What do you mean by soon? 3 months, 3 years, 30 years? The time it takes to solve them will make a big difference to your decision making in the present moment. Our current feeling is that whilst they might be reduced and mitigated in different ways, fixing them completely is going to be very hard as in many ways they are a feature, not a bug, of the way LLMs work.

Because of all the above problems, at this point we came to the conclusion that it would not be possible to use LLMs in the way of traditional software, where you automate it and forget about it. Instead we would have to design a different system that would include humans at various vital points.

We tried this, and the problem was it took more time for teachers to read all the essays, read the AI feedback and edit the errors than it would have taken for them to provide the feedback themselves in the first place.

There is also a paradox here that LLMs that are 80% accurate might end up leading to better overall system performance than LLMs that are 98% accurate. That’s because at 80% accuracy, the human in the loop knows they have to stay alert as the errors are coming along fairly frequently. If the errors come along less frequently but are still present, they are more likely to have switched off.
In both these cases, a relatively simple and naïve form of “human in the loop” is not good enough. It’s not enough to just have a human overseeing or checking.

So we moved instead to asking LLMs to comparatively judge essays. We know that humans are much better at Comparative Judgement (CJ) than they are at absolute judgement – and it turns out LLMs prefer CJ too! They do still make unusual errors that humans don’t make, but we can use human judgements and our statistical model to identify and eliminate such errors.
